newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to give $15 million more in N. Korea aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to give $15 million more in N. Korea aid.

text.p: The United States is expected to provide $15 million in additional food aid to famine-threatened North Korea, administration and congressional sources said on Tuesday.
The new contribution, being offered on the eve of crucial talks on the future of the Korean peninsula, was expected to be announced by the State Department later in the day.

It will bring the total U.S. food aid to the isolated Stalinist regime to $33.4 million since late 1995, including $10 million announced in February. The aid is being given in response to a U.N. World Food Program appeal.

In talks opening in New York on Wednesday North Korea is to tell the United States and South Korea if it will agree to a year-old proposal for peace talks aimed at replacing the Korean War armistice with a durable peace treaty.

U.S. officials insist such food donations are based on humanitarian assessments but Pyongyang has made clear repeatedly that its food shortage is so dire it could not consider the peace talks until food aid was made available.

The World Food Program recently called for $95.5 million for 200,000 tons of food. But North Korea is believed to be nearly out of food stocks and has said its requirements for the year could be as high as 2 million tons.

After some skepticism about the extent of the problem, the Clinton administration and members of Congress have increasingly expressed concern a severe food shortage in the impoverished state, caused largely by two years of floods.

"By all accounts, the situation is worsening. It is dramatically worse than it was several months ago or even four or five weeks ago. At least our assessment of it is dramatically worse," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Monday.

In visits to Pyongyang and three southern agricultural counties on March 15-18, inspectors with the World Food Program found signs that efforts to deal with two consecutive years of crop-killing floods were breaking down.
Children were malnourished and many were stunted while the populace in general was living on rations of 3.5 ounces (100 grams) of rice per day, or about one bowlful.

Many people were reported to be surviving on this rice, plus stores of dried vegetable leaves, ground corncobs and ground sweet potato stalks. Small irregular farm markets had formerly provided some food but most have closed as surpluses have dwindled, the inspectors said.
This dire picture was reinforced by several senators who visited North Korea recently and said they were convinced the country has a very serious food shortage problem.

And Rep. Tony Hall, who made a separate trip there, reported that "North Korea is rapidly descending into a hell of severe famine". The Ohio Democrat said it was clear that even Pyongyang's military was suffering the effects.
